profile.name: Native Hawaiian (Kānaka Maoli)
profile.region: Hawaiian archipelago / Pacific; US-HI used as a geographic navigation region
profile.kind: Indigenous people / language / diverse communities and institutions
profile.overview: Begin with annotated public sources on Native Hawaiian identity, language education, land and water care, institutional roles and the 1993 federal apology. This initial source guide supports a Hawaiʻi map connection while keeping its limited coverage visible.

sections.title: An Indigenous people and a Hawaiian name
sections.text: Native Hawaiian and Kānaka Maoli identify the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi. A University of Hawaiʻi publication uses Kānaka Maoli in that sense, while the 1993 federal apology resolution defines Native Hawaiian for its own purposes through descent from the islands’ aboriginal people. These sources provide an introduction to names, rather than a universal enrollment test. Birthplace or residence in the present state alone does not supply the ancestry described in that resolution.

sections.title: A homeland connection for the map
sections.text: The resolution explicitly connects Native Hawaiian ancestors with the area now constituting the State of Hawaiʻi. The state index therefore provides a useful route to this people’s sources. It should not be read as a parcel map or a determination of territorial rights. Community and family histories require closer island-specific research.

sections.title: The Kingdom, overthrow and a dated apology
sections.text: The 1993 resolution records Congress’s account of United States diplomatic and military participation in the 1893 overthrow, and apologizes to Native Hawaiians for the resulting deprivation of self-determination. It also expressly declines to settle claims against the United States. Reading those provisions together prevents an apology from being mistaken for a comprehensive legal resolution. Kingdom history, subsequent annexation and present political proposals need additional original documents and Hawaiian scholarship.

sections.title: Rebuilding everyday language education
sections.text: ʻAha Pūnana Leo traces its work to Hawaiian language educators who organized in 1983. Its account describes the first preschool at Kekaha, Kauaʻi, in 1984, followed by schools on other islands. Elders’ advice about children learning through everyday interaction shaped that work. The history also acknowledges inspiration from Māori language nests. This is a community institution’s account of rebuilding education; the page does not establish current proficiency outcomes for all Native Hawaiians.

sections.title: Learning through care for land and water
sections.text: Paepae o Heʻeia’s public collection explains how a coastal fishpond on Oʻahu uses a wall and managed water exchange to support aquatic life. Its education page describes students investigating water quality and other ecological questions while helping inform the organization’s management decisions. These accounts connect inherited environmental knowledge with contemporary learning at one place. Heʻeia’s story should not be generalized to every island, family or fishpond.

sections.title: Understanding OHA as a particular institution
sections.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs describes itself as a semi-autonomous state agency. Its account connects its creation with 1970s Native Hawaiian activism and the 1978 constitutional convention. It identifies advocacy, research, land management and support for community programs among its roles. Reading its own description helps distinguish a service and advocacy institution from the people as a whole. Its remit does not establish consensus on political futures or make OHA a sovereign Native Hawaiian government.

sources.title: Public Law 103–150: acknowledgment and apology for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo
sources.annotation: Original 1993 federal resolution, including historical recitals, an apology, its own definition of Native Hawaiian and a disclaimer that it does not settle claims. Read as a dated primary instrument, not a complete history or a determination of contemporary sovereignty, citizenship or remedies.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual five-page PDF text/OCR read: 107 Stat. 1510–1514, all recitals and sections 1–3. This records text inspection, not a claimed page-image transcription audit.

sources.annotation: Brief university publication identifies Kānaka Maoli as the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi through an attributed alumna’s reflection. Included for naming and orientation only; its brevity makes it supporting material rather than a substantive research-target source.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual definition and attributed reflection, lines 34–49. Embedded video and linked dictionary were not reviewed.

profile.relationshipNote: Native Hawaiian / Kānaka Maoli is a people-level access point, distinct from the population of the modern state and from any single agency or organization. OHA is a state agency; ʻAha Pūnana Leo and Paepae o Heʻeia are specific community institutions. The historical Kingdom, its subjects, Indigenous identity, ancestry-based program categories and contemporary political proposals require their own contexts. The state-index connection does not decide recognition, citizenship or territorial claims.
researchGaps: A fuller account needs Hawaiian-authored historical scholarship and original Kingdom-era documents, with island-specific histories.
Contemporary family voices, diaspora experiences, health and housing, and the diversity of political positions need stronger representation.
Legal program definitions, current law and recognition debates require separately dated specialist research; the 1993 resolution does not answer them all.
Learning outcomes, restoration results and present program availability have not been independently assessed.
evidenceNotes: Four substantive works/collections and one short supporting naming reference were inspected within recorded scopes on October 21, 2026. Paepae o Heʻeia pages count once. The guide is not promoted to a developed profile or an adequate initial introduction; no community review is implied.
No generated images, copied photographs, restricted cultural content or precise site coordinates were used. The 1993 law was reviewed as text/OCR, not asserted as a full image-transcription audit.
